title: CLO Master Express Lesson 27 | Advanced Tutorial on Fabric Texture Processing (Jacquard Metallic Sequins)
transcript:
First of all, today we are going to give you a course on texture processing.  
We will introduce the following four aspects.  
First, we will review the concept of fabric pre-processing and fabric images.  
In this session, we will introduce three fabric processing methods,  
which include the processing methods for three types of fabric,  
and also the processing method for a highlight map.  
Let's get started today.  

First of all,  
after obtaining a piece of fabric, we need to smooth it out, then clean up the floating layer and loose threads.  
At the same time, we can use a scanner to scan the fabric after setting the DPI parameters to get a smooth fabric pattern.  
The recommended DPI setting is between 300 and 600.  

In CLO, we will use the following types of patterns:  
First, the pattern that shows the floral shape and color of the fabric itself.  
It can be a floral pattern or a flat pattern obtained by scanning.  
Another basic pattern is a blue-orange hairline pattern.  
The second pattern demonstrates how to add hairline patterns.  

There are three patterns on the DPI chart.  
I used two, four, and seven;  
I used five and added one hundred.  
Here are some examples to create texture processing effects by adding an illusion image.  

Next, we will also apply transparent images.  
In transparent images,  
we have transparent images in RGB mode  
and transparent images in alpha mode.  
I will introduce them later.  

Let's take a look at the highlight map in the lower left corner.  
The highlight map helps us define the roughness of the fabric.  
The closer to the black area,  
the stronger the reflection and the brighter the effect.  

On the right side,  
after adding the highlight map,  
we add the metal map  
to create an image with a metallic sense.  

There are already some scanning machines on the market,  
such as Visu and Shidi,  
which are from the same brand.  
These scanning machines are a collaboration of software and hardware.  
They can scan the texture map, the line map,  
and the metal map we need.  
If you are interested,  
you can learn more about them.  

If you only have software like Photoshop (PS) and PixPlant,  
you can use some of the operating methods introduced in today’s course.  

Let's look at the first piece of material and see how it looks.  
In the first piece,  
we will use a green material with a sculpting effect.  
The parameters are on the right side.  
Let's go through the specific operation steps.  

First, open the texture image in PS.  
After opening it,  
unlock the layer.  
Then, use the transparent cutting tool  
to select the endpoint of the circular unit.  
You can zoom in and adjust the position of this endpoint.  
Try to select the position of the shoulder, which is close to the pixel.  
After clicking OK,  
you get an image of the four continuous sides.  
Use the position function to check if this position is appropriate.  

Adjust its parameters.  
Pull the slider to the right,  
then move the image’s pixels downwards.  
Check the trace on the side.  
If it is stuck,  
is it because of your own network?  
What I show here is normal.  

Now, we are using the clone tool.  
I used the shortcut key “S” to shrink my brush.  
Near the area, select a similar pixel point,  
and paint over it.  
This way, we can cover the trace on the pattern.  

Near the corner, we can copy the image on the right side.  
Then click the left button near the base and copy it.  
Paste it where we need to cover.  
We can see the trace is gone.  
So, use shortcut keys to control the brush.  

Now, use the shortcut key to hold onto the pattern.  
Then, check if the background is consistent.  
If we want to fill empty spaces, copy surrounding pixels and paint them.  
Shrink the view and check if any other changes are necessary.  
Name this Fabric 1.  

Next, make a line drawing of this pattern.  
Use the filter to find the 3D production line drawing.  
Choose the opposite height based on the actual effect to get a line drawing with embossing.  
At the same time, adjust the detail shrink.  

After making the line drawing, we need to give it an embossed effect to make it three-dimensional.  
To do this, we create a calligraphy effect.  
Copy the pattern,  
then press Shift + Ctrl + I to invert the colors.  
After that, adjust the color levels.  
When adjusting color levels, be sure to blur the colors if necessary.  

I suggest choosing “scandal” (possibly a filter or effect),  
adjusting the high sp nadern and sharp dull as shown in the video.  
The base pattern of this silk texture gives a bit of texture to the leaves.  
The part going down is a texture of non-woven fabric, so we still need to create a rough surface map.  
It is still a logical image.  

Then adjust its color.  
After adjustment, use the invert function.  
You can also press Ctrl + I to do this.  
At this point, the texture contrast might not be strong enough, so adjust the curve to increase highlights and shadows, then adjust the color.  

After that, to achieve a gentler gloss, apply a high-definition blur with a blur value set to 1.  
Save all these images one by one in the preset file folder.  
Hide the layer,  
open CLO, and find the first project file.  

This is an wither (probably "outerwear").  
We can apply the texture on the fabric.  
Set its type as silk satin to obtain the texture effect on the fabric.  
Since the fabric surface is very clear, strengthen the hairline intensity.  
Set changeability to 2.  
Let's look at the output effect first.  
It is a little thick, so lower it a bit.  

The texture of the fabric is relatively wide and its area is large.  
So I did not increase the particle diameter beyond 4.  
This reduces the computing load on the computer.  
It can also be set to 2.  
We can achieve the desired fabric style.  

Next, add a surface roughness map.  
You can clearly see that the output part is brighter, glowing,  
while the base texture is dull.  
At the same time, we can set the roughness.  
The larger the value, the weaker the reflection.  

If the surface roughness is not enough, go back to PS and adjust it.  
Move the left end of the curve to the right to darken the black parts.  
Replace the previous image.  
Return to CLO, press F5 to refresh.  
You will see the brightness come out.  

Click on actual rendering,  
adjust parameters,  
set intensity to 60,  
reflection intensity to 75.  
This makes the fabric style closer to reality.  

After completing the texture, save the fabric to the Fabric1 folder.  

OK, next,  
the fabric we need to process is translucent with a floral pattern.  
Parameters are listed on the right.  
Let's demonstrate.  

Open the Fabric2 folder,  
find the scanned pattern.  
Select a color that is more even and a clearer texture.  
Select a square continuous pixel point.  
I found a protruding point.  
Since the circle is very small, enlarge the selection area.  
You can see the location of the protruding point is very thin.  
Find a similar pixel point on the right side of the water level as a circular unit.  

Use the five-point repair tool to clear dark pixels in the image.  
This completes the texture operation.  

Next, find the splinter area.  
Check the width according to pixels.  
Use the clone tool to copy the splinter marks.  
Copy the upper pixel and apply a coating to cover.  

Set the scan resolution to 300; 300 is generally sufficient.  
I suggest using very clear textures like these:  
- This texture  
- Or this texture  
- Or this texture  
I suggest copying the image below and extending it upward in order to complete a continuous splinter connection.  

Apply it in the splinter direction to show the texture more evenly.  
You can change the position again.  
Check if more obvious splinter points remain.  

Now adjust position parameters to place the pattern.  
I suggest cutting the circular unit pattern into different parts.  
For example, from right to left is the second pattern.  
The blurred areas correspond to the protruding circle, the clearer areas to the flower pattern.  
Cut the flower pattern as a section.  

Copy the pattern to create a discovery image.  
Use the 3D filter to find a discovery image for smart production.  
Adjust contrast details for desired discovery intensity.  

Next, make a drawing.  
Make a frame for the hairball.  
You can also use an irregular drawing for the protruding circle, but the current method is more convenient.  
Alternatively, draw the discovery image by hand.  

The last step is to apply a high-definition blur.  
Review:  
The discovery image’s white parts are the protruding circle,  
black parts are not protruding.  
To smooth edges, use high-definition blur.  
Choose the radius based on texture style (e.g., 3).  

Give the picture a new name.  
Keep the blur pattern below.  
You can also use a transparent image.  

Now, create this transparent image.  
Use the decoder to select irregular, opaque areas.  
Press SHIFT to select irregular shapes at once.  
Re-select the shape, then press CTRL + SHIFT + I to invert the selection.  
Adjust image contrast and colors.  

The triangle on the right indicates highlight counts,  
the middle gray levels,  
and the left black dots indicate dark spots.  
Adjust image colors accordingly.  

After selection, deal with shadow parts.  
Cover unadjusted shadow areas,  
duplicate nearby silhouettes and pixels.  
Use the rectangle tool to do this.  
This makes the simulation more realistic.  

Zoom in slightly to see obvious bulges.  
The image’s colors are varied, so do not worry about the number of highlights.  
Tip: Add shadows first.  
There are three colors here; the shadow color is in the middle, so the shadow is centered.  
After adding shadows, light and dark colors blend.  

Then add shadows.  
When saving in PS, save the visible image only.  
Hide upper layers,  
save as JPG.  

Open CLO, go to Fabric2 folder, open second project file.  
This is a linked group.  
Drag finished texture image directly to material application.  
Click OK.  

Zoom in on sleeve details.  
The added texture is flat.  
Add hairline image and increase hairline strength for more definition.  
Set change degree to 0.8.  
Because change degree is small, reduce particle diameter for more realistic rendering.  
Change points are scattered, so continuous lines are not kept open, saving computer operation and increasing speed.  

Here, use RGB transparent image.  
Explain that transparent images are divided into two types: RGB mode and alpha mode.  
In RGB mode, provide a grayscale map.  
Closer to black means more transparent, closer to white means less transparent.  
Alpha mode uses the alpha channel information in the image.  
Areas without pixels appear as clouds with 30% black opacity.  

Next, change the color inside the circle.  
Change the model on top and the circle below.  
Use the eyedropper tool to extract blue from the page.  
Adjust to fit, then add the color to the palette for later use.  

Open the line; the clothing bottom group color is changed.  
Change the lace color and surface line color as well.  
Return to the front view of the model to see the final outfit look.  
Look at the details; this is the final look.  

Now, the third fabric piece: a flat fabric with a black pattern and some metallic threads.  
Look at the final outfit look.  
To save time, I will show a picture of the outfit.  
This is the basic pattern.  
Rename it.  

Next, make a line drawing.  
Using a filter to create a line drawing, the black outline is obvious.  
Adjust black color using the color selection tool.  

(Repeated mentions of using the color selection tool omitted for brevity.)  

Shrink the brush size using shortcut keys: medium with the middle key, smaller with the left key, larger with the right key.  
After reducing the gray area, create a path for the selected area.  
Why create this path?  
Because the black area needs roughness treatment, and we also need to create a metal pattern or other patterns, so repeat selection is necessary.  
Use auto-create path function to quickly select areas.  

Remove the whole picture, then create the 3D hairline.  
Adjust detail shrink parameter, increase blurring slightly.  
Click OK to get a clearer hairline.  
Hairline can be selected, easy to make simple paper patterns with Americorch.  

Create hair using traditional style.  
This time, we make a doll.  
Although I don't have a doll, I want to make one.  
Let's see the current step.  

Use a pen, select the empty circle in the lower right corner to convert the path into a selection.  
This is a quick simulation.  
Select again, use color range to darken the selection slightly.  
Combine with marquee selection tool to remove unnecessary parts.  
Press Delete to get an image with transparent pixels.  

I am making an alpha mode transparent image.  
It's best to use alpha mode transparent images to make grids more delicate and structure more detailed.  
Put a darker background underneath, for example, a card behind the material to scan.  
This helps with color range selection.  

Next, make a roughness map.  
Make hidden parts bright and other parts dark.  
Copy original pattern and remove color.  
Adjust color range, choose an area with many flowers.  
Use path tool to switch from selection to quick selection.  
Adjust output color range to make it closer to the bottom pattern.  

Use quick selection tool to select reflection areas, i.e., metal thread regions reflecting light.  
Deepen this area and adjust color range to darken.  
Keep metal thread texture; maintain gray value as part of it.  

Thus, create a rough map for the surface.  
Blur pixels slightly for softer reflection.  

Finally, remove the metal thread parts above in CLO.  
Since each fabric type can only be set once, we remove the metal thread on top.  
To create reflective effects for metal thread texture, add a hard highlight.  

Select the yellow part with strongest reflection.  
Make a loop; smaller brush size means smaller pixels.  
After selecting metal thread part, press Ctrl + C and Ctrl + V to copy and paste.  
The pasted pixels appear on a new layer.  

Name this PNG image and save all fabric images to Fabric3 folder.  
Paste fabric photos and PNG alpha images with transparent channels into Fabric3 folder.  
Also paste surface roughness and final print images.  
If there is a transparent background, save as PNG format in PS.  

Open Fabric3 folder and open third costume set.  
Apply these texture images to the top clothing.  
Adjust mode to alpha mode.  
The 3D window changes accordingly.  

After placing images, add a print.  
Set the print to metal type for a metallic texture.  
In the 3D window, click actual rendering to check effect.  
If the print does not align with the yellow pattern, select the print file in the text editor and move it to the appropriate position.  
Return to 3D window and check rendering again.  

Adjust material parameters:  
For surface roughness, increase roughness and brightness.  
Set strength to 60.  
For reflection strength, set to 60 to make material brighter and more transparent.  

The metal texture surface becomes very hard and bright.  
To get a more beautiful and realistic metal texture, adjust surface roughness and reflection strength.  
If originally metal, reflection should be 100%, but reduce slightly here.  
Adjust metal level to get fabric texture without harsh effect.  

Use auto-generated image function to increase image strength.  
Use pattern color to auto-generate the discovery map for texture display.  

Next, the fourth fabric piece with metal texture.  
It may not be very clear; let's look at operations together.  

This is a transparent mesh background.  
First, make a cross-sectional cut using a transparent cutting tool; find contact points through displacement.  
After confirmation, use copy-paste tool to paint contact points and cover marks.  

After processing contact marks, use displacement to check for unprocessed areas, double displacement to determine pixel positions.  
Since the picture needs cutting, set all four corners of the lace to color blocks without mesh or fine texture details.  
This helps with subsequent drawing.  

First, finish the bottom layer texture.  
Select unnecessary black mesh parts with quick selection tool; use small brush to quickly select areas.  
Press Delete to remove selection.  

For hard-to-select lace parts, use multiple selection tools.  
I suggest using a set of locks to hook along edges for quick selection.  

After selection, check if any area is selected.  
Perform reverse operation to select lace flower shape.  
Create a work path, switch to selection state, then copy and paste.  
This creates the lace flower shape on the upper layer.  

Fill the bottom pattern with white for observation.  
Delete excess black pixels using color range selection.  
Adjust contrast to a larger range, maximum 200, minimum 0; suggest 100-150.  

Adjust to one color, reduce dark sides in the middle, brighten the bottom.  

Adjust pink flowers.  
Scan changes color to rose gold.  
Select flower parts accordingly.  

Since lace involves repeated selection switching, use auto-generated path as introduced before.  
Select needed area for quick selection, go to path, name the work path, then generate a new path.  
Convert work path to selection.  

Adjust the lace pattern on the upper layer by pulling the dark side of the color range to the right to restore strength and adjust color balance to get a pink effect closer to real fabric.  

Now, the upper lace layer is done.  
Next, process the mesh part.  
Mesh is delicate, so use selection tool to find a suitable range, find a circle, define as pattern, use paint bucket tool to fill with foreground color.  
Get a particularly uniform mesh.  

Similarly, use color range to adjust contrast, make black selection, confirm, quickly remove black parts by pressing Delete multiple times.  

Now, get this mesh.  
Adjust to match white bottom pattern by adjusting color range and removing color.  
Fill foreground color as black to get uniform mesh.  

Now, merge the first and second layers of this pattern to form a composite fabric result.  
Repeat for second layer.  

Review:  
Two layers—first and second—merged to composite fabric.  

Third and fourth layers:  
The fourth layer is a pied with blue choking (possibly a typo or technical term).  
Set to reverse height, adjust blurring degree, reduce details.  
Click OK to get the line drawing.  

Next, create an illusion drawing.  
First define the line drawing, then define the logic drawing.  
Use the work path to convert flower path into black, select other areas and fill with white.  
Be sure not to miss any fill.  

After coloring, cancel selection, apply filter to blur pixels and enlarge them.  
Create an illusion drawing with rough surface.  
Blur helps get a more flat texture effect so protruding parts are even.  

Next, create metallic feeling for the pink part.  
Use the path to remove white part of lace, fill base pattern with black to create matte metallic look.  
Highlight metallic feeling on white lace parts by sharpening and adjusting color.  
Keep lace area small with gaps to enhance metallic feeling in bright spots.  

The metallic pattern is ready.  
Apply and try to bold it.  
Now done.  

Go to component picture style, add an outline.  
The images are ready to be fixed.  

Now, save these fabric images in the FibreCAD4 folder.  
Also save the displacement map (called "Displacement" or renamed to "Dis").  
Save surface roughness, hairline, and texture.  
Generally, hairlines are saved as JPG, but this time PNG was used.  
For more even JPG hairlines, use scanned colors close to fabric color.  

Use a previously used group to apply textures.  
Group divided into fabric and material; apply to fabric.  
Add hairline and adjust intensity (increase for obvious style).  
Add displacement map, visible only in rendering window; do not adjust displacement parameters immediately.  
Add color fill to hairline, add surface roughness.  

Check effect; color may be too thick.  
Adjust with fill tool to lighten.  
Finish editing this part.  

Go back to PS and adjust luminosity.  
Adjust density; density higher in model than picture.  
Since hair color is darker, adjust again as needed.  
Fill gray area; if too dark, use lighter gray.  

At this point, transparent picture format should be JPG, corresponding to RGB transparent mode.  
Save texture and apply it to background.  
Background texture looks normal, closer to material color.  
Lace fabric looks closer to real effect.  

Original metal gloss is weak; change fabric to metal type.  
Set changeability.  
Reduce particle diameter for smooth texture effect.  
Keep continuity open for natural crevice effect.  

After setting to metal type, adjust surface roughness to reduce strength and smooth texture.  
Reduce reflection intensity for self-darkening and gloss effect.  
Since metal silk texture exists, increase metallicity slightly.  
However, increasing metallicity darkens flower shape, making it foggy.  
Control metallicity carefully.  

Add metallic pattern to brighten metallic silk backlight on pink embroidery.  

Now, metallic silk backlight effect is basically done.  
Some reflections vary with light color, so add hard highlights.  
The highlights are detailed; practice if needed.  

Enlarge painting area.  
Use color range (found in dropdown menu) to select brightest highlight parts.  
Narrow color range to isolate brightest area.  
Switch workflow to define selection area.  
Select white pixels in selection.  
Reduce color range to get zero-star pixel selection.  
Copy and paste on new layer.  

Take black pixels, return to underlayer, fill black pixels to better see hard layer.  
Want to simulate light, but light spots shouldn’t be too large or dense.  
If too dense, repeat selection and erase excess pixels with the eraser brush.  
Select correct layer before erasing to preserve star effect.  

Making texture takes patience; the prepared texture images are complex.  
Mainly to introduce flexible applications in CLO.  
Practice and adjust as needed.  

After cherry blossom image is done, save as PNG.  
Back to CLO, add it as cherry blossom fabric to clothes and fabric documents.  

A small trick:  
Set cherry blossom type to “light.”  
When light is on, reflection increases.  
I set it to metal to show difference between metal and light.  
Metal mode shows gray area, convenient for matching cherry blossom shape.  

Metal effect is hard, closer to fabric texture.  
For real fabric effect, recommend setting type to light.  
If you want to know light attributes in CLO, watch lesson three of our master course.  

Don’t forget to add replacement images for cherry blossoms to current pattern.  
Metal texture is hard; adjusting reflection or metallic degree makes texture harder.  
Set to light for softer, surface-closer look.  

Adjust color intensity and transparency to get fabric texture effect.  
Set light value to 1; observe effect.  

Now the pattern is done.  

Next, the last topic: processing a light pattern.  
Operate in PS; parameters listed on the right.  

First, make a circular cut.  
Then, use image drawing tool to paste and copy desired places.  
Use fabric background color near the area, press Alt and left-click to copy selection.  
Adjust brush to soft light area.  

When copying light, set flow to 100% for transparency.  
Copy similar color light, then cover it.  
This completes the texture at intersections.  

This is a small light film trick; zoom in to see details.  

Next, copy silver part of second half of film.  
Increase brightness of bright areas.  

After processing four-way sequence, check for other areas needing pasting.  
When making light film, not only check four-way sequence, but also paste white light film with copy tool.  
Copy light film colors.  

For example, make white light more transparent, so dark areas have white light, white areas have black light.  
This makes lighting appear more realistic.  

Press Alt to copy vertical logical areas, paint downwards, cover bright white spots with black.  

For all fabric processing, make a circular cut of the first four continuous steps.  
Only after completing the bottom layer pattern will the back images be successfully made.  

Now generate the discovery map for this image; share a trick.  
Since bright spots are basically on a flat surface, even with different lights, they remain bright spots.  
Colors of different bright spots vary greatly.  

Without color now, see a result neither black nor white.  
We need to brighten white to create a more uniform discovery map from the same background.  

Use color range to select colors.  
Adjust color degradation, select different colors.  
Check if all areas are selected; if not, invert black areas.  
Selected area becomes brighter white; whole picture looks gray and flat.  

Create uniform discovery map, adjust detail collection parameters until satisfied, then click OK.  

Copy bottom layer texture.  
Make rough surface map, rename as “rough.”  
Rough surface map: closer to black is brighter, closer to white is rougher.  

Adjust color interface accordingly.  
Brighter white means rougher, darker black means flatter.  
Select and adjust curve and contrast.  

After inversion, get surface roughness.  
Make bottom pattern matte, bright areas have bright texture.  

After surface roughness is done, add metal pattern.  
Metal pattern makes bright areas brighter and dark areas subdued, adding depth.  

After adjusting color, save metal pattern.  
Create new layer to duplicate bright areas (white parts).  

Why?  
Because in the last fabric pattern, light type was used.  
Bright parts reflect light.  
Use light type to make print pattern, making texture more realistic.  

Choose color, remove black parts, save step.  
Self-define flower pattern removed, fill transparent layer as print pattern.  

Bottom layer is white, so print is subtle.  

Save these fabric patterns in Fabric5 folder.  

As you see, flowers are no longer white, and color varies.  
Flower color differs from background color, but overall harmony is maintained.  

Open fifth project file in Fabric5.  
Apply light texture on top (vest style).  
Paste as texture, adjust hairline, reduce length to 5.  
Add rough texture on surface.  
Reduce length, set light texture to metal.  
Add metal image.  
Observe light texture effects.  

Add texture of light; rough surface disappears when light is added.  
Adjust light texture.  

Last step: add hard highlights to special bright pixels.  
Set attribute to light.  
Effect visible only in rendering.  

In attribute editor, select light and position appropriately.  
Distribute evenly on material, apply and close.  

View effect after application.  
Open actual rendering to check.  

Since bits are thin and concentrated, no need to add new canvases.  
Lower metal level to reduce hardness.  
Effect shows backlight surface fully.  

View final rendering effect.  

Today's tutorial is nearly complete.  
Save object to Fabric5 folder.  
Today's tutorial is over.  
Thank you for watching.

chunks.content: # CLO Master Express Lesson 27 | Advanced Tutorial on Fabric Texture Processing (Jacquard Metallic Sequins) This document details advanced fabric texture processing techniques in CLO, focusing on fabric pre-processing, texture map creation, highlight and metal maps, transparent images, and multi-layer fabric effects for realistic rendering of jacquard metallic sequins and other complex textiles. --- ## Fabric Pre-Processing and Image Acquisition This section covers fabric preparation, scanning parameters, and basic pattern types essential for texture processing in CLO. - **Fabric Preparation**: Smooth the fabric, clean floating layers and loose threads before scanning. - **Scanning**: Use a scanner with DPI set between 300 and 600 to obtain smooth, high-quality fabric pattern images. - **Pattern Types in CLO**: - **Base Pattern**: Shows floral shapes and colors; can be flat or floral, obtained from scanning. - **Hairline Pattern**: Adds texture detail, often blue-orange colored. - **Highlight Map**: Defines fabric roughness; black areas indicate stronger reflection and brighter highlights. - **Metal Map**: Creates metallic effects on fabric surfaces. - **Scanning Devices**: Brands like Visu and Shidi offer hardware-software integrated scanners that capture texture, line, and metal maps. - **Software Alternatives**: Photoshop (PS) and PixPlant can be used for manual texture processing if scanning hardware is unavailable. --- ## Processing the First Fabric: Green Sculpted Silk Satin This section explains step-by-step texture editing and map creation for a green silk satin fabric with sculpted effects. ### Photoshop Editing 1. **Texture Image Preparation**: - Open texture in PS, unlock the layer. - Use the transparent cutting tool to select a circular unit near the shoulder area for pixel accuracy. - Check alignment with the position function. 2. **Cleaning and Cloning**: - Use the Clone tool (`S` shortcut) to cover traces and seams. - Copy and paste image portions near corners to cover marks. - Fill any empty spaces by cloning surrounding pixels. 3. **Line Drawing and Embossing**: - Apply 3D production line drawing filter. - Adjust opposite height and detail shrink parameters to get embossed, three-dimensional lines. 4. **Calligraphy Effect for Embossing**: - Copy pattern and invert colors (`Shift + Ctrl + I`). - Adjust color levels and blur as needed to soften edges. - Use filters such as “scandal” (likely a stylized effect) to enhance texture. 5. **Texture Contrast and Gloss**: - Adjust curves to increase highlight and shadow contrast. - Apply high-definition blur (blur value = 1) for gentler gloss. 6. **Saving**: - Save all intermediate files into the preset folder. ### CLO Application - Set fabric type to **silk satin** for texture effect. - Increase hairline intensity and set changeability to 2. - Limit particle diameter to 4 or 2 to reduce computational load. - Add a **surface roughness map**: - Larger roughness values yield weaker reflections. - Adjust roughness map in PS by darkening black parts if needed. - Adjust rendering parameters: intensity 60, reflection strength 75 for realism. - Save processed fabric to **Fabric1 folder**.

chunks.content: ### CLO Application - Set fabric type to **silk satin** for texture effect. - Increase hairline intensity and set changeability to 2. - Limit particle diameter to 4 or 2 to reduce computational load. - Add a **surface roughness map**: - Larger roughness values yield weaker reflections. - Adjust roughness map in PS by darkening black parts if needed. - Adjust rendering parameters: intensity 60, reflection strength 75 for realism. - Save processed fabric to **Fabric1 folder**. --- ## Processing the Second Fabric: Translucent Floral Pattern This section outlines the processing of a translucent fabric with floral patterns, including handling splinters and transparent images. ### Texture Editing in Photoshop 1. **Selecting Continuous Pixel Areas**: - Choose even color and clear texture areas. - Use transparent cutting tool to select circular units, enlarging selection for small protrusions. 2. **Repair and Cleaning**: - Use five-point repair tool to remove dark pixels. - Clone splinter marks to cover damaged areas. 3. **Scan Resolution**: Set to 300 DPI for clarity. 4. **Extending Splinter Connection**: - Copy base textures upward to create continuous splinter lines. 5. **Pattern Segmentation**: - Cut circular units into sections (e.g., flower pattern separate from blurred areas). 6. **Discovery Image Creation**: - Use 3D filter to generate discovery map for embossed effect. - Adjust contrast for desired intensity. 7. **Drawing Hairballs and Protrusions**: - Frame hairballs with regular or irregular drawings. - Optionally draw discovery image manually. 8. **High-Definition Blur**: - Blur edges with radius ~3 pixels for smoothing. 9. **Transparent Image Creation**: - Use decoder to select irregular opaque areas. - Invert selection (`Ctrl + Shift + I`) and adjust contrast. - Handle shadows by duplicating nearby pixels and covering unadjusted areas. 10. **Saving**: -
